title: Houthis Strike Riyadh's Airport and an Aramco Refinery as NATO Opens Steadfast Noon After Russia's Nuclear Warning
subhead: Houthi drones and missiles hit King Khalid International Airport and Saudi oil infrastructure, killing at least three, while NATO begins its annual nuclear exercise and its military chiefs gather in Kyiv for the first time.

sections.heading: Houthis Hit Riyadh Airport and an Aramco Refinery
sections.body:
Saudi authorities said at least three people were killed in attacks on two of the kingdom's international airports, including Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, according to AFP. Al-Monitor reported that a plane was damaged and left billowing smoke at Riyadh airport, and a witness told the Associated Press that parts of the airport were evacuated. The Houthis also claimed strikes on an Aramco refinery and other sites, Reuters reported via CNA, and explosions were heard across the Saudi capital.

The Houthis issued what Times of India described as a 'last warning to global airlines' over Saudi airspace, a direct threat to civil aviation rather than just shipping. Flights were disrupted and Saudi Arabia began rallying allies, the Straits Times reported. This is a qualitative jump: the group is now demonstrating the reach to strike the Saudi capital's core infrastructure, not only Red Sea shipping or border towns.
sections.whyItMatters: Attacks on the Saudi capital's main airport and an Aramco refinery show the Houthis can penetrate Saudi air defences and threaten both Gulf oil output and civil aviation. That widens a conflict the kingdom had hoped to contain and pushes up the risk premium on Gulf energy.

sections.heading: Trump Rules Out Iran Strikes Before the Midterms as Tehran Prepares for a Long War
sections.body:
President Trump said the US will not resume military strikes on Iran before the November 3 midterm elections, the Seattle Times reported, citing AP. Oil prices fell from their daily highs on the remark, according to Invezz. The same day, Iran International reported that Tehran says it is ready for a prolonged war, and a Soufan Center brief noted both Washington and Tehran appear to be preparing for renewed combat after the election.

Trump's decision effectively puts a six-week political freeze on the largest active front. But Iran International reported that Tehran sees the gap between talks and war narrowing, and the Seattle Times noted Iran has been scaling up Hormuz attacks to raise pressure on Trump as the vote nears.
sections.whyItMatters: The pause is political, not strategic. It buys Washington calm markets through the vote while leaving the underlying deadlock unresolved, meaning the post-election window is where escalation risk is concentrated.

sections.heading: US Opens Direct Talks With Myanmar's Generals
sections.body:
The Trump administration has begun direct talks with Myanmar's military-installed government, reversing years of US efforts to isolate the generals who seized power in the 2021 coup, Reuters reported via CNA, the Bangkok Post and ThePrint. The outreach is being led in part by Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance, the Jerusalem Post reported, and has focused first on shutting down scam centres that target Americans. Mining.com.au reported the talks also cover rare earths.

The move follows a rare US visit to Myanmar in September to free an American businessman, Reuters reported. It signals Washington is willing to engage the junta pragmatically, trading legitimacy for cooperation on criminal networks and critical-minerals supply.
sections.whyItMatters: Engaging a sanctioned junta and discussing rare earths shows the US prioritising supply-chain security and borderless crime over its democracy-and-sanctions posture. It also hands Beijing and the region's armed resistance a signal that Washington is willing to deal with Naypyidaw directly.

sections.heading: NATO Opens Nuclear Drill and Sends All 32 Military Chiefs to Kyiv
sections.body:
NATO began its annual nuclear exercise, Steadfast Noon, after Russia's warning over Kaliningrad, the Washington Post reported. In parallel, military representatives from all 32 NATO member countries arrived in Kyiv for the first time, according to Ukranews, as the alliance's Military Committee met on air defence and hybrid warfare, the Brussels Times reported. The NATO summit in Ankara concluded with a focus on defence manufacturing and military supply chains, Berlin Today reported, with Macron pushing European defence autonomy there.

A Stars and Stripes report warned that Russia's 'shadow war' campaign of sabotage and hybrid attacks has NATO on the defensive. Rubio said US pressure on allies to raise defence spending is 'not hostile', the Los Angeles Times reported.
sections.whyItMatters: Running a nuclear exercise while Russia brandishes its own nuclear signalling is a deliberate demonstration of resolve in the Baltic and Kaliningrad theatre. Sending all 32 military chiefs to Kyiv for the first time signals NATO is institutionalising its support for Ukraine even as a US-brokered peace push stalls.

sections.heading: US-Russia-Ukraine Peace Push Stalls as Envoys Pitch 'New Ideas'
sections.body:
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said Moscow has no plans to resume peace talks with Ukraine, RBC-Ukraine reported, and the Kyiv Independent reported that US and Russian officials have confirmed Trump's latest Ukraine peace push is falling apart. On the US side, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet Ukrainian negotiators and European officials in Miami to present 'new ideas and proposals', Axios reported. Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said Kyiv is ready for trilateral talks in October and that five ceasefire formats are on the table, according to Ukranews.

Zelensky sent a delegation to meet the Trump envoys and hinted at secret US-Russia economic talks, the Kyiv Independent reported. The Kremlin said a comprehensive settlement is necessary, Anadolu reported. The two sides are still describing talks in different terms, with Moscow cool and Washington presenting fresh ideas.
sections.whyItMatters: The diplomatic track is not dead but it is not moving: Moscow says no, Washington is proposing, Kyiv is positioning. With winter approaching and Russia striking Ukrainian infrastructure, the gap between the rhetoric of talks and the reality of the front line is the core risk.

sections.heading: Oil Tops $104 as Hormuz Attacks and a Gulf Storm Collide
sections.body:
Brent crude rose above $104 during the session before easing, with Anadolu reporting a nearly 4 percent gain on Middle East tensions and US supply concerns, and the Economic Times noting crude near $102 on ship attacks. Investing.com and Epoch Times attributed the spike to a double supply threat: fears of strikes on Iran and Hurricane Isaias. Fortune tracked the day's price, and Phil Flynn's energy report described rising risk waves across the market.

The move captured a market split between fear of a supply shock and weakening demand forecasts, Bellwize noted. Oil pulled back from its highs after Trump ruled out near-term strikes on Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: Energy is again pricing geopolitical risk directly: ship attacks, strike fears and a Gulf hurricane are all hitting supply expectations at once. For importing economies this is an inflation tax that arrives just as the US heads into midterms.

bottomLine: The day's clearest escalation came from the Houthis, whose strikes on Riyadh's international airport and an Aramco refinery showed they can reach Saudi core infrastructure and threaten civil aviation, killing at least three. On the Iran front, Trump froze US strikes until the November 3 midterms while Tehran signalled readiness for a long war, shifting escalation risk into the post-election window. NATO opened its Steadfast Noon nuclear drill and sent all 32 military chiefs to Kyiv for the first time, hardening its posture as the US-brokered Ukraine peace push stalled and Moscow said it had no plans to resume talks. Washington also reversed years of policy by opening direct talks with Myanmar's generals over scam centres and rare earths, and oil briefly topped $104 on the combined shock of Hormuz attacks and a Gulf storm. The through-line is political timing: Washington is buying calm before its midterms while adversaries and allies alike reposition for what comes after.
